lines: Welcome to Module Four: Deployment and Scaling.
A demo agent is easy; surviving real traffic is not.
Picture an online retailer whose shopping agent runs smoothly for a hundred users.
Then Black Friday arrives, with fifty times the traffic.
First, the GPUs run out of memory.
The culprit is the KV cache, which holds every token each conversation has already seen.

say.1: The culprit is the kay-vee cache, which holds every token each conversation has already seen.

lines: Then latency explodes.
Long prompts are slow to process, so the first word of each reply takes seconds.
Kubernetes was set to add pods when CPU usage climbs.
But CPU sits at twenty percent while the GPUs are saturated, so nothing scales.
Each new GPU pod takes minutes to pull its image and load the model.
By the time they're ready, the shoppers are gone.
Then a shipping tool slows down, with no timeout.
Workers hang waiting on it, until none are left for anyone else.
The agent retries, its HTTP client retries too, and the load multiplies.
On the busiest day of the year, the agent goes down.
Every one of those failures has a known fix.
Lesson one starts inside the GPU, where each request runs in two phases.
Prefill reads the whole prompt at once, limited by compute.
Decode writes one token at a time, limited by memory bandwidth.

say.0: Pree-fill reads the whole prompt at once, limited by compute.

lines: You'll see why the KV cache, not the weights, limits how many users fit.
And how continuous batching and prefix caching win back speed and capacity.

say.0: You'll see why the kay-vee cache, not the weights, limits how many users fit.

lines: Lesson two scales two tiers: cheap orchestration pods, and costly GPU inference.
Inference scales on queue depth or latency, never CPU, with warm replicas to hide cold starts.
It also cuts cost by routing easy requests to a smaller model.
And it measures cost per completed task, not per token.
Lesson three keeps the agent alive when tools break.
Timeouts, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers, and a fallback, such as a cached answer.
This domain is thirteen percent of the exam, and it rewards the right signal and the complete answer.
Next up, lesson one: inside the GPU.
